Reputation Management for Public Figures and Influencers

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

Public figure reputation management is about speed and preparation: an influencer, athlete, presenter or artist lives under constant scrutiny, so the work starts long before any controversy by cleaning old content, securing accounts and agreeing a response protocol. When something does break, the first hours decide whether it stays a comment thread or becomes a news story with lasting search results.

Why public figures face a different level of risk

A public figure's name is searched far more often than a company's, and every search result is read as a statement about the person. Journalists, fans, critics and brand managers all look at the same page one, the same Instagram grid and the same AI-generated summaries, so a single negative item travels further and faster.

Italian law also treats well-known people differently. Courts recognise a wider margin for criticism and reporting when the information concerns a person's public role, which means that some unflattering content is lawful and will stay online. Private life, health, family and children remain protected, and the line between the two is where much of the practical work happens. Understanding that line early prevents wasted removal attempts and shows where real protection is possible.

Old posts and the archive problem

The most common source of a crisis for creators is not something new but something old: a joke from 2014, a comment on a football match, a photo from a party, rediscovered when the person becomes more visible. Archive screenshots spread even after the original is deleted.

Auditing your own history

A structured audit reviews every account the person has ever used, including forgotten ones on platforms that are no longer popular, plus old blogs, forum profiles and video channels. Each item is classified as fine, to archive or delete, or to address publicly if it is likely to resurface. This is done privately and before a major milestone, such as a television contract or a sponsorship launch.

What deletion can and cannot do

Deleting your own content is always allowed, but copies saved by others remain. For items already republished by third parties, the options are a request to the site, a right to be forgotten request when the material is outdated personal data, or a short, honest acknowledgement that takes the surprise out of the story. Celebrity reputation management often relies on the third option, because a statement made calmly in advance carries more weight than a defence written under pressure.

Fake accounts, impersonation and deepfakes

Impersonation is a constant problem for well-known people: fake profiles ask fans for money, promote investment scams or post offensive content in the person's name. In Italy this can amount to the offence of identity substitution (sostituzione di persona, art. 494 c.p.), and platforms in the EU are obliged under the Digital Services Act to act on valid notices.

The practical defence combines prevention and fast reporting:

  • obtain verification badges on every major platform and link all official profiles from one website;
  • publish a clear statement of which accounts are official and that the person never asks for money;
  • use each platform's impersonation form, attaching an identity document when requested;
  • report manipulated videos and voice clones, especially sexual or scam content, through the dedicated policies, and file a complaint with the Polizia Postale when fans are being defrauded.

Deepfakes created with AI tools add a new layer, since a realistic fake video can circulate before anyone checks it. Having official channels where the person can deny quickly, and a team that knows the reporting routes, reduces the window in which a fake is believed.

Brand partnerships and commercial transparency

For influencers, reputation and income are directly linked: brands check search results, comment sections and past collaborations before signing, and contracts increasingly include morality clauses that allow termination after a scandal. Influencer reputation management therefore includes protecting the commercial side.

Undeclared advertising is a frequent trigger of criticism and of regulatory attention. In Italy, the Autorità per le Garanzie nelle Comunicazioni (AGCOM) has issued guidelines that apply rules on commercial communication to influencers with large audiences, and the advertising self-regulation code requires clear labels such as "#adv" or "pubblicità". Partnerships with brands that later face their own scandal can also damage the person, so a short check of the partner's search results and reviews before signing is part of good practice.

For a creator, a transparent label on a sponsored post costs nothing; an accusation of hidden advertising can cost several partnerships at once.

Rapid response when criticism goes viral

When a controversy starts, the goal in the first hours is to understand it before reacting. A rushed post, a deleted comment noticed by followers or an aggressive reply to a journalist turns a limited discussion into a second, larger story.

SituationUsual first stepWhat to avoid
Legitimate criticism of something said or doneShort, sincere acknowledgementConditional apologies, blaming fans
False rumour or fake screenshotFactual denial with evidence on official channelsRepeating the rumour in detail
Coordinated harassmentModeration tools, reporting, evidence collectionEngaging individual attackers
Defamatory articleLegal assessment and request for correctionPublic threats against the outlet

Long-term protection of the search footprint

After the peak, attention moves to what remains in Google and in AI answers. News articles about the controversy can rank for the person's name for years, so a steady flow of new, accurate material, such as interviews, project pages, an official website and well-kept profiles, gradually defines what people see first.

Older articles may later qualify for delisting if the story has lost relevance and the person's role has changed, as explained in our article on what the right to be forgotten really removes.
